more.summary: Dr. Arthur Tiutenko from FAU and colleagues from LMU München and the South African National Museum in Bloemfontein discovered a new species of snake in the Harenna Forest, on the southern slopes of Ethiopia's Bale Mountains: Dasypeltis albigularis, or the white-throated egg-eater. "Three other new species in this genus are still waiting in line," the zoologist adds.

more.title: Lonely shoppers demonstrate less compassion in their purchases than others, study shows
more.summary: Chronically lonely people are less likely to buy products that benefit others, such as fair-trade or child-labor-free goods, according to a new study by researchers at Concordia and the University of the Fraser Valley. The team ran four studies involving more than 1,400 participants across North America.

more.summary: Open data from NASA’s Fermi mission helped an international team of scientists develop a method for finding pulsars about a million times faster than before.

more.title: computor: AI tutor as a programming learning aid
more.summary: Artificial intelligence is now capable of writing entire computer programs. This poses a challenge for university education. How can students still learn to program for themselves if an AI can do the work for them? Students should be able to use AI tools effectively, but they must also understand how programs work and how to troubleshoot errors.

more.title: Extreme weather poses growing risks to global oil and natural gas shipping, new IEA report finds
more.summary: Extreme weather events are posing significant risks to international oil and natural gas shipping, with the potential to damage critical infrastructure, disrupt major trade routes and threaten energy security, according to a new IEA report.

more.title: AI virtual cell technology could reveal how genetic changes and drugs alter cells
more.summary: Today's artificial intelligence models can predict whether someone with a genetic change will develop a disease, but cannot answer two critical questions: Why did the disease occur, and how do we design a treatment?

more.title: Building structured-light systems in three dimensions
more.summary: Structured light has become an important tool across modern optics. By shaping properties such as amplitude, phase, polarization and spatial mode, researchers can create light fields with capabilities beyond those of conventional laser beams. These engineered light fields are finding applications in communications, imaging, sensing, optical computing and quantum photonics.

more.title: New mondo grass species found in Yunnan
more.summary: Botanists have described a new Ophiopogon species from the Yunnan Wenshan National Nature Reserve in southeastern China. They named it Ophiopogon longiscapus for its unusually long flowering stalk, or scape.

more.title: Organizational science offers new lens for studying extremism
more.summary: Accepting the Republican nomination for president in 1964, Barry Goldwater declared, "I would remind you that extremism in the defense of liberty is no vice!" His statement illustrates how the cause being defended can shape judgments about the actions taken in its name.

more.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
more.summary: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin.

more.title: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history
more.summary: A bizarre whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so dramatically crooked that scientists believe it may have been the most asymmetrical of any mammal. Discovered in Peru, the extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo had an enormous downward-curving snout and a skull so distorted that researchers initially thought it had been damaged after death.

more.title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
more.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large.

more.title: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible
more.summary: Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible depending on something unexpected: tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air. Scientists say this discovery could help make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors.

more.title: Climate communication that resonates must be based on empathy
more.summary: Climate change is a global reality, but people often encounter it through different local realities. For some, it enters everyday life through social media feeds, news reports, scientific findings and public discussion. For others, it is through water scarcity, food insecurity, floods, heat waves, wildfires or the loss of a home or a loved one.

more.title: Putting Google's AI hurricane model to the test
more.summary: A week before Hurricane Melissa slammed into Jamaica last fall, the forecast models couldn't agree on where it was headed or how strong it would get. One got it right—an AI model from Google DeepMind, which called both the storm's path and its Category 5 strength.
